blurb.en: Say hello the local way, greet elders first, and close a talk politely.
Keep any conversation alive when you don't understand yet.
Answer the first questions everyone asks: name, home, work, family.
Ask prices, bargain fairly, count, pay and get change.
Agree a fare, give directions to a driver and get off where you want.
Get help fast, and handle the pharmacy and the doctor.
Order, say how you like it, and be a good guest at someone's table.
Visit a family home, honour the elders, and leave well.
Make a plan on the phone: when, where, and 'I'll call you back'.
Say how you are, talk about the day, and react like a friend.

ar-EG.note: Works with anyone, any time. The religious greeting is st-0039.
عامل إيه؟ / عاملة إيه؟ (3aamil eeh / 3amla eeh) is the same question, also daily. Polite form with حضرتك for elders and strangers.

en.text: I'm fine, thank God. And you?

ar-EG.note: Adapted: Egyptians answer 'how are you' with 'thank God', not 'thank you'.
Literally 'gently a little'. Only 'please' changes with the listener.
Egyptians call their speech عربي (Arabic). مصري (masri, Egyptian) is also heard.
The everyday way to ask what a word means.

en.text: How do you say this in Arabic?

ar-EG.note: Literally 'what is this called in Arabic'. For a feminine thing: دي اسمها إيه بالعربي؟ (di ismaha eeh).
لو سمحت (st-0013) works as 'please' too; both are taught.
Gets attention, and also means 'please'.
Adapted: when offered something, 'yes, I'd love that'. Egyptian Arabic uses one form here for everyone.
'This' agrees with the thing: دي بكام؟ (di bi-kaam) for a feminine thing.
مية = water (mayya). The same letters also spell 'hundred' (miyya); the sound tells them apart.
In Arabic only 'sorry' changes, with the speaker.
The reply is صباح النور (sabaa7 en-nuur), never a copy. Egyptian Arabic uses one form here for everyone.
Egyptian Arabic uses one form here for everyone.
The reply is مسا النور (masa n-nuur). Egyptian Arabic uses one form here for everyone.
The reply agrees with the person who wished it: وإنت من أهله (w-inta min ahlu) to a man, وإنتي من أهله (w-inti min ahlu) to a woman.
يا جماعة = 'everyone'. Walking into a room, many people say السلام عليكم يا جماعة instead.
Literally 'we are honoured'.
The usual reply is نهارك سعيد back, or 'you too' (st-0035).

Adapted: leaving work or a visit in the evening, Egyptians say 'goodbye, good night'. ليلتك سعيدة (leltak sa3iida) is a written or TV wish that hotel and shop staff use; colleagues at the office door don't say it.
To an elder or a stranger of standing, use the حضرتك form.
Literally 'a thousand thanks'.
على إيه؟ (3ala eeh, 'for what?') is the warm everyday alternative.
In Arabic 'sorry' follows the speaker only. معلش (ma3lish) is the softer 'sorry about that'.
Adapted: Egypt has no fixed elder greeting. The respect is حضرتك (your presence) plus يا حاج / يا حاجة for an older man or woman.

en.text: Good morning. I slept well, thank God.

ar-EG.text: صباح النور. نمت كويس، الحمد لله.
ar-EG.translit: sabaa7 en-nuur. nimt kwayyis, el-7amdu lillaah.
ar-EG.note: صباح النور is the fixed reply to 'good morning'. Egyptian Arabic uses one form here for everyone.

en.text: Good morning! How did you sleep?

ar-EG.note: Asked by family and close neighbours; others just ask عامل إيه؟
Plural form when a family arrives together.

en.text: Can you write it for me?
Speak to me in Arabic, please.

ar-EG.note: أهلي = my family, my people.

en.text: This is my first time here.

ar-EG.note: Swap in the learner's own job; most job words add -a for a woman.
عيال = kids, casual. ولاد (wilaad) is the neutral everyday word; see st-0177.
Literally 'I have thirty years'.

en.text: How long have you been here?

ar-EG.note: Swap in any produce. Prices are per kilo at a souq stall.
'That' agrees with the thing: here the price (masculine). For a feminine thing: دي غالية أوي (di ghalya awi).
Scaled to Egyptian pounds: the market scene is thirty a kilo, offer twenty, last price twenty-five, two kilos fifty.
Scaled to Egyptian pounds (two kilos for fifty).
إديني is the same for a man or a woman seller, so this line has one form.
'One' agrees with the thing: واحدة for a feminine thing (a watermelon, a bag), واحد (waa7id) for a masculine one.
'This' agrees with the thing: هاخد دي (di) for a feminine thing.

en.text: Do you have a bigger one?
Do you have change for two hundred?

ar-EG.note: Scaled: the two-hundred-pound note is the one sellers struggle to break for a small buy.
Wallets and InstaPay are the usual phone payments; cash is still king at a souq stall.
Handing over money or a thing.
خلي is the same for a man or a woman, so this line has one form.

Adapted: sellers say 'at your command, what will it be'. يا باشا to a man and يا مدام to a woman are friendly titles for any customer. Sellers also say يا حاجة to an older woman, and some say يا هانم.
Scaled to a realistic Cairo tomato price (thirty pounds a kilo).

en.text: Okay, how much will you pay?

ar-EG.note: آخر كلام = 'last word', the seller's final price.
Also heard, and the same for everyone: أي خدمة تانية؟ (ayy khidma tanya?)
Two kilos at twenty-five = fifty. Keep the scene's arithmetic true.
Literally 'there is no change'. Heard every day.
Agree the fare first for a tok-tok or taxi; microbus fares are fixed.

en.text: Take me to the market, please.

ar-EG.note: وديني is the same for a man or a woman; only 'please' changes.
Adapted: 'to the side here' is how you stop any ride. To a driver, يا أسطى (ya usta) replaces 'please'.
هدي is the same for a man or a woman; only 'please' changes.
هو = 'it', for a masculine place. For a feminine one: هي بعيدة؟ (hiyya bi3iida).

en.text: Is this the way to the hospital?

ar-EG.note: وقت ('time') keeps it from sounding like 'how much does he charge?'

en.text: Which microbus goes to the market?

ar-EG.note: Adapted: the shared microbus replaces the bus.
Literally 'which way do I go?'
Adapted: a driver names the fare with a title, not 'please': يا باشا to a man, يا مدام to a woman.
Plural: shouted to everyone around.
The ambulance number in Egypt is one two three.
The police number in Egypt is one two two.
حالة طوارئ means a state of emergency (the news, a curfew), and الطوارئ alone is the emergency room.
Older people also say الأجزاخانة (el-agzakhaana).
Cairenes say they feel تعبان ('unwell, tired'). The shorter أنا تعبان is st-0211.
عندي حرارة (3andi 7araara) is also common.

en.text: Do you have something for a headache?
Three times a day, after food?

ar-EG.text: تلات مرات في اليوم، بعد الأكل؟
ar-EG.translit: talat marraat fi l-yoom, ba3d el-akl?

ar-EG.note: The police station is called القسم.
Adapted: what a pharmacist really says. يا فندم is a polite 'sir / madam' and fits everyone. Egyptian Arabic uses one form here for everyone.
Literally 'the medicine, is it for you (polite)?' A pharmacist who opens with يا فندم keeps حضرتك.

en.text: Take two tablets, three times a day.

ar-EG.text: خد قرصين، تلات مرات في اليوم.
ar-EG.note: قرصين = two tablets.

addressee_f.text: خدي قرصين، تلات مرات في اليوم.

ar-EG.note: At the ahwa people order واحد شاي (waa7id shaay), 'one tea'.
Coffee means Turkish coffee unless you say otherwise.
لبن = milk in Egypt.

en.text: Just a touch of sugar, please.

ar-EG.note: Adapted: sugar is ordered by level. سادة (saada) none, على الريحة (3ala r-rii7a) a touch, مظبوط (mazbuut) medium, زيادة (ziyaada) sweet.
سادة = no sugar.
حبة صغيرين = 'a tiny bit', the everyday phrase when more is served.
For one dish, 'it' agrees with the dish: ده حلو أوي / دي حلوة أوي. Thank the cook with st-0161.
الحمد لله، شبعت (el-7amdu lillaah, shibi3t) is the same for everyone and also common.
لحمة = red meat. To rule out chicken too: مباكلش لحمة ولا فراخ (mabakulsh la7ma wala firaakh).
Literally 'is there chili in it?'
Literally 'bless your hand'. The fixed thanks to the cook.
Accepting an invitation is always softened with 'God willing'.

en.text: What would you like, tea or coffee?
How do you take your sugar?

ar-EG.note: Adapted: 'how do you take your sugar?' The answer is a level (st-0151).

en.text: Would you like something to eat?

ar-EG.note: واحد = one more glass or cup.
Literally 'light us up again'.
Literally 'what's the family's news?' Egyptian Arabic uses one form here for everyone.
Use the حضرتك form to an elder.
Respect: يا حاج / يا حاجة to an older man or woman.

en.text: The journey was good, thank God.
She's well. She sends her greetings.

polite.text: كويسة، الحمد لله، وبتسلم على حضرتَك.

polite_f.text: كويسة، الحمد لله، وبتسلم على حضرتِك.

ar-EG.text: ما شاء الله، بيتَك حلو أوي.
ar-EG.note: Praise always starts with ما شاء الله, which wards off envy.

addressee_f.text: ما شاء الله، بيتِك حلو أوي.

en.text: May God give you long life.

ar-EG.note: A blessing for an elder: use the حضرتك form. ربنا يخليك (rabbina ykhalliik) is the everyday short one.

en.text: Yes, we have to go. Thank you for everything.

ar-EG.text: أيوه، لازم نمشي. شكراً على كل حاجة.

en.text: Sit down. How was the journey?

ar-EG.text: اتفضل اقعد. الطريق كان عامل إيه؟
ar-EG.note: In Cairo 'the road' mostly means the traffic.

addressee_f.text: اتفضلي اقعدي. الطريق كان عامل إيه؟

addressee_pl.text: اتفضلوا اقعدوا. الطريق كان عامل إيه؟

ar-EG.note: والدتك = your mother, the respectful word.
Literally 'you're leaving this early?'

en.text: The network is bad. I'll call you back.

ar-EG.note: Literally 'the charge is nearly finished'.

en.text: I'll be there in ten minutes.
Let's meet at ten in the morning.
Let's meet at the metro station.

ar-EG.note: Adapted: in Cairo people meet at a metro station. محطة الأتوبيس (bus station) works the same way.
نمرة = phone number, the everyday word.
For a meeting Egyptians say 'I'll be present' (موجود), which follows the speaker. The English line has no gender; the Arabic does.

en.text: A little. Can we talk later?
Yes, it's too hot for me.

ar-EG.note: الدنيا ('the world') is how Egyptians talk about the weather.
Literally 'a masterpiece'. حلو أوي! (7ilw awi) also works.
Literally 'the place here pleases me'.
The fixed wish for anyone who is ill. The reply agrees with the person who wished it: الله يسلمَك (allaah yisallimak) to a man, الله يسلمِك (allaah yisallimik) to a woman.
The reply agrees with the person who said it: الله يبارك فيك (allaah yibaarik fiik) to a man, الله يبارك فيكي (allaah yibaarik fiiki) to a woman. Egyptian Arabic uses one form of مبروك for everyone.

en.text: What did you do on your days off?

ar-EG.note: Adapted: 'what did you do on your days off?' Egypt's weekend is Friday and Saturday. Cairo says agaaza, and many people text it الأجازة.
كانت agrees with الإجازة (the days off).

en.text: Fine, thank God. What did you do on your days off?

ar-EG.text: كويس، الحمد لله. عملت إيه في الإجازة؟
ar-EG.translit: kwayyis, el-7amdu lillaah. 3amalt eeh fi l-agaaza?
ar-EG.note: Cairo says الإجازة as agaaza, and many people text it الأجازة.

speaker_f.text: كويسة، الحمد لله. عملت إيه في الإجازة؟
speaker_f.translit: kwayyisa, el-7amdu lillaah. 3amalt eeh fi l-agaaza?

addressee_f.text: كويس، الحمد لله. عملتي إيه في الإجازة؟
addressee_f.translit: kwayyis, el-7amdu lillaah. 3amalti eeh fi l-agaaza?

both_f.text: كويسة، الحمد لله. عملتي إيه في الإجازة؟
both_f.translit: kwayyisa, el-7amdu lillaah. 3amalti eeh fi l-agaaza?

en.text: Sit down. How was the journey?

ar-EG.text: اتفضلوا اقعدوا. الطريق كان عامل إيه؟

en.text: She's well. She sends her greetings.

ar-EG.text: كويسة، الحمد لله، وبتسلم على حضرتِك.

en.text: Good morning! Need anything from outside?

ar-EG.text: صباح الخير يا أستاذ! محتاج حاجة من برة؟
ar-EG.translit: sabaa7 el-kheer ya ustaaz! mi7taag 7aaga min barra?

addressee_f.text: صباح الخير يا مدام! محتاجة حاجة من برة؟
addressee_f.translit: sabaa7 el-kheer ya madaam! mi7taaga 7aaga min barra?

ar-EG.text: أيوه، إن شاء الله. الساعة كام؟
ar-EG.translit: aywa, in shaa2 allaah. es-saa3a kaam?

blurb.en: Morning on the stairs of a Cairo apartment block or at the building door, where the bawwab (doorman) sits and the neighbours pass.
A vegetable stall at the neighbourhood souq, priced per kilo in Egyptian pounds, where fair bargaining is normal.
A tok-tok through the side streets (agree the fare first) or a microbus on a fixed route (pass your fare forward).
The ahwa, the street coffee house: plastic chairs on the pavement, tea in glasses, Turkish coffee, sugar ordered by level.
The corner pharmacy, open late, where the pharmacist is the first stop for a small health problem.
A Friday visit to relatives with a box of sweets: greet the elders first, eat what is offered, leave slowly.
A call that opens with alo, makes a plan with 'God willing', and fights a weak network.
A day at the office after the Friday and Saturday weekend, with tea brought round by the office helper.

meaning.en: Nothing gets done without other people's help; work together.
Live within your means; spend only what you have.

proverbs.literal: Stretch your legs as far as your blanket reaches.

meaning.en: Children take after their parents; like father, like son.
Every parent thinks their child is beautiful; love is blind.

proverbs.literal: In his mother's eyes the monkey is a gazelle.

proverbs.text: اللي بيته من إزاز ما يحدفش الناس بالطوب.
proverbs.translit: illi beetu min izaaz ma yi7difsh en-naas bi-t-tuub.

meaning.en: Don't criticise others for faults you have yourself.

proverbs.literal: Whoever's house is made of glass shouldn't throw bricks at people.

meaning.en: Choose your neighbours before you choose your home; good neighbours matter most.
Be patient and the hard time will pass.

proverbs.literal: Patience is the key to relief.

meaning.en: Let the past go; forgive and move on.
You got lucky once; don't keep taking the same risk.

proverbs.literal: The clay jar doesn't survive every time.

proverbs.text: اللي على راسه بطحة بيحسس عليها.

meaning.en: A guilty person gives himself away by being touchy.

proverbs.literal: Whoever has a bump on his head keeps feeling it.

proverbs.text: الباب اللي يجيلك منه الريح سده واستريح.
proverbs.translit: el-baab illi yigiilak minnu r-rii7 siddu w-istirii7.

meaning.en: Cut off the source of your trouble and you will have peace.

proverbs.literal: The door the wind comes through, shut it and rest.

meaning.en: Live honestly and no one can find anything against you.

proverbs.literal: Walk straight and your enemy will be puzzled by you.
